method: The published high-altitude charts give a per-unit adjustment for three bands, and the page holds them as pairs so both ends of each published range survive. At 3,000 ft: liquid +1 to 2 tbsp per cup, leavening -1/8 tsp per tsp, sugar 0 to 1 tbsp less per cup, flour 0 to 1 tbsp more per cup, oven 15 to 25 °F hotter. At 5,000 ft: liquid +2 to 4 tbsp, leavening -1/8 to -1/4 tsp per tsp, sugar 0 to 2 tbsp less, flour 0 to 2 tbsp more, oven 15 to 25 °F hotter. At 7,000 ft: liquid +3 to 4 tbsp, leavening -1/4 tsp per tsp, sugar 1 to 3 tbsp less, flour 2 to 4 tbsp more, oven 15 to 25 °F hotter. The page computes with the midpoint of each range and reports the resulting minimum and maximum too. An elevation between two bands is interpolated linearly; 7,000 ft and above hold the top band; below 3,000 ft nothing is changed, because that is where the published chart starts. Each adjusted amount is the entered recipe amount moved by the per-cup rate: leavening and sugar down, liquid and flour up, and the oven temperature up by the midpoint 20 °F. Amounts are US cups of 16 tablespoons, leavening is teaspoons and temperatures are Fahrenheit; the page converts feet to metres and °C at the edges. Yeast-bread proofing times, canning and pressure-cooking adjustments, and the choice of flour protein are outside the page.

sources.title: University of Wyoming Extension, B-1310 — "Cooking and Baking It Up! Altitude Adjusters": per-cup liquid, leavening, sugar and flour adjustments at 3,000, 5,000 and 7,000 ft and the 15-25 °F oven increase
King Arthur Baking — "High-Altitude Baking": the same adjustment table with a leavening chart and the advice to change one ingredient at a time, starting with the smaller adjustment
